Here's the plan for today. First, a quick look at what AI actually is. Then three parts: the input, the model, and the output. In between, there are four live demos, and they tell one story. I'll pretend I'm a lecturer from KAED, with a paper, getting ready for a conference. Demo one, context engineering: an AI that knows my paper. Demo two, prompt engineering: a photo-like image for my poster, from a SketchUp model. Demo three: a diagram of my method for the poster, one I can still edit. Then agents, AI that actually does things, and then the main event: video. There are two very different ways AI can make a video, pixels or code, and today is about code. And demo four, motion design: a short video for my talk, made with code, step by step. Every step is on the slides, so you can do it again at home. And if we have time, a bonus.

Okay, quick one before we start. All of these are AI. Every one of these names. Let's go through them.

Hands up: who has heard of these? ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok. Okay, most of you.

How about these? Opus, Sonnet, Astra, DeepSeek, Argon, which is Google's newest Gemini model. These are the actual models running behind those chatbots.

And these ones? Qwen, GLM, MiniMax, Kimi, Mistral. Anyone?

And these? Whisper, YOLO, Kokoro. These aren't chatbots at all. Some of them turn speech into text, some find objects in a picture, some make voices and music. Actually, the video you just watched was made with a few of these. So there's a whole zoo of AI out there, and every few months there's a new name.

So all of these are what we call AI. As an engineer, my main problem is this: a client comes to me with a business challenge, and I need to map that challenge onto an AI concept and work out how AI can automate it.

So when a client comes in, it's usually one of these. Machine learning. Deep learning. Anomaly detection. Time series. Computer vision. NLP, natural language processing. And generative AI.

And each of these goes deeper. Computer vision, which is my own area, has classification ("what is this?"), detection ("where is it?"), segmentation ("exactly which pixels?"), and pose estimation ("how is it standing?"). Generative AI is where you make new things. Images, from GANs back in the day to the diffusion models now. And text, with large language models.

So today, the path we're taking is this. From AI, we go into generative AI.

Inside generative AI, we go into large language models.

And from large language models, we get the chatbots that everyone uses. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok. That's our focus today.

(Optional: click any node.) And if you're wondering where your own work fits, say you're doing object detection, it's here: AI, computer vision, object detection.

It all goes in the square hole.

Back in the day, each of these jobs needed its own kind of model. Its own specialists, its own tools, its own training data.

Answering questions? That's a language model, an LLM. Square peg, square hole. Of course.

Object classification, "what's in this photo?" That's a computer vision model. Right there, its own box... nope. LLM. The big chatbots can see now.

Speech to text. Speech recognition model? LLM.

Translation. LLM.

Sentiment analysis: is this review positive or negative? LLM.

Reading a scanned form. LLM.

(Play.) It all goes in the square hole. Today you can do every one of these with one large language model. It's not always the cheapest or the best way, but it works. So that's where we're going to keep our focus today.

The AI system lifecycle, as used by the OECD and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (simplified).

Remember, as an engineer, my job starts with a problem. So here's what a real AI project looks like. This is the AI system lifecycle, the one the OECD and the US standards body NIST use. From left to right. First, plan and design: what's the problem, and what does success look like? Then collect the data. Then build the model. Then verify and validate: does it work, and is it actually right? If not, we go back. Then deploy it, put it to use, and it starts giving answers. And then operate and monitor it, because the world changes, the data drifts, the goal changes. And we go round again.

Today, we're not doing the whole cycle. We're going to zoom in on the middle. The data is the input. The model is the model. And when it's deployed, what it gives back is the output. Input, model, output. That's the part that explains how AI works, and how you map a problem to it.

Typically you have the input. That's what you give it: text, a picture, your voice, or just numbers.

You have the model. That's the part that does the work. It learned from lots of examples, and inside it's really just billions of numbers.

And you have the output. What you get back: an answer, a picture, a voice, or a prediction like a price. These three things are basically what we'll cover in this workshop. We'll go through them one by one, starting with the input.

A 1,100 sq ft house in Gombak. What's the rent?

Illustrative figures, not market data. Only size is used; rooms and location would add more inputs.

Let's start with a classic example. Here's the question: a 1,100 square foot house in Gombak, what's the rent? Given x, what's y? The size is our input, x. The rent is the output we want, y.

To answer it, we need examples. Every dot here is a house we already know the size and the rent for.

Then we pick a model. The simplest one there is: linear regression. Find the straight line that best fits all those dots. That line is the model. And a straight line is just this equation from school: y equals m x plus c. Here, rent equals one times the size, plus 300.

And out comes the price. Put 1,100 into the equation: 1,100 plus 300. A 1,100 square foot house in Gombak, about RM 1,400 a month. And here the input is, well, numbers. Pretty straightforward.

2 · Input · image
a photo
one pixel = one number
0 = black · 255 = white
Model

So what about images? Here's a cat.

To a computer, this picture is just a grid of tiny squares, pixels.

And each pixel is just a number, from 0 to 255. Zero is black, 255 is white, and everything in between is a shade of grey.

And those numbers are what we feed into the model. That's how you represent an image as numbers so the model can take it as input.

2 · Input · video
A video is just pictures, shown fast
4 pictures a second

Slow: you see each picture.

24 a second: your eye sees movement.

Each picture is a frame. Films use 24 frames a second; phones and YouTube often 30 or 60.

And video? A video is just pictures. Here are twelve of them, a ball bouncing.

If I show them slowly, four a second, you see each picture. A flipbook.

Now twenty-four a second. Same twelve pictures. And now your eye sees a ball bouncing. Each picture is called a frame. Films are 24 frames a second; your phone usually records 30 or 60. So for a model, a video is just a stack of pictures, and each one becomes numbers, like the cat. Most models don't even look at every frame: Gemini, for example, takes about one frame a second, plus the sound.

2 · Input · voice
−1 to +1every number sits somewhere in this range
Model

Same thing with voice.

Sound is just a wave, and we measure the height of that wave thousands of times a second.

Each of these dots is a number. Zero is silence, the middle line. Plus one is the wave pushed all the way up, minus one all the way down. So your voice becomes a long list of numbers between minus one and one.

And again, those numbers go into the model.

2 · Input · text
5 tokens
Malay, same meaning: 7 tokens
Model
Real token IDs from OpenAI's open tokenizer (o200k_base). Other companies' models split text differently.

And last but not least, words. This is what the chatbots work with.

A sentence gets chopped into pieces called tokens. Sometimes a whole word, sometimes part of a word.

And every token is just a number in a big dictionary.

And look what happens in Malay. "Saya sayang kucing saya." Same meaning, but more tokens. "Sayang" and "kucing" get chopped into pieces, because these models learned mostly from English.

And those numbers are what go into the model. So whether it's a picture, a voice, or a sentence, by the time it reaches the model, it's all numbers.

(Say it, no slide.) A quick reminder before we move on. Everything you type or upload goes to someone else's servers, often outside Malaysia. So leave out personal data: student names, IC and matric numbers, grades, health records. Leave out confidential work: unpublished results, exam papers, and manuscripts or grants you're reviewing. Elsevier, for example, tells reviewers not to upload a manuscript into an AI tool at all. Remove names and IDs before you paste, and check the setting that lets them train on your chats. And if you're not sure, leave it out.

3 · Model
What's inside a model

every line is a parameter, a knob the model learned

So what's actually inside a model? Remember our inputs: the rent, and the photo of the cat. Both became numbers. So where do those numbers go? Let's open a model up.

Here. It's layers. Those numbers come in on the left: that's the input. Each layer passes numbers on to the next, layer after layer, and the answer comes out on the right. A big model like Llama has 126 of these layers.

And every one of these lines is a knob, which we call a parameter. Training is just adjusting those knobs, again and again, until the output comes out right. So when people say a "7 billion" model, they mean 7 billion knobs.

So how big are these models?

A small one like Google's Gemma 4, about 5 billion, fits on your phone.

31 billion needs one graphics card. Each little square is one big GPU, just to hold the model in memory.

Then it jumps. DeepSeek's V4 Flash is 284 billion. Four GPUs.

V4 Pro is 1.6 trillion. Twenty.

And Kimi K3, from Moonshot in China, is 2.8 trillion. Thirty-five GPUs, just to load it. That's the biggest model anyone has released openly so far.

And the best ones, GPT, Claude, Gemini? They don't tell us. The companies keep that secret. Outside estimates put them in the trillions too, so probably somewhere around here.

So what does it take to build one of these? Here's a model where the company actually published the numbers. Meta's Llama, 405 billion parameters.

They trained it on over 15 trillion tokens. To give you a sense of that: all of English Wikipedia, every article, is about 5 billion words. So that's like reading the whole of Wikipedia about two thousand times.

On more than 16,000 top-end GPUs, running for months. Every one of these dots is a GPU.

All together, that's about 22 gigawatt-hours of electricity. That square on the left. And the one next to it is what the whole of Malaysia uses in one hour. About the same. One model, one training run.

And it produced almost nine thousand tonnes of CO₂. About the same as 1,900 cars driving for a whole year.

Let's stay on electricity, but over a whole year. The International Energy Agency says a typical AI data centre uses as much electricity as a hundred thousand homes, and the biggest ones being built, twenty times that. The cluster that trained Llama, run for a year, is this little square. xAI's Colossus 2 passed one gigawatt this year; run flat out for a year, that's more than all of Brunei. The whole country.

And if we zoom out: here's Malaysia, the whole country. And here's every data centre in the world, in 2024. About twice Malaysia. And it's still growing fast.

And back when GPT-4 was trained, Sam Altman said it cost more than 100 million dollars. So this is not something a university builds. That's why we use these models instead.

Now here's the interesting one. Back in late 2024, DeepSeek, a Chinese lab, released a model that competed with the best. And they did it on the H800, a nerfed version of Nvidia's chip, because of US export restrictions.

They said the final training run cost about 5.6 million dollars. Compare that with "more than 100 million" for GPT-4.

When their reasoning model R1 came out in January 2025, Nvidia lost 589 billion dollars of market value in a single day. The biggest one-day drop in history. Because people suddenly asked: do you really need all that hardware?

Now to be fair, that 5.6 million is just the final run. It doesn't include all the research and experiments before it. But still, it showed that clever engineering can beat brute force.

3 · Model
Frontier, closed
use it through their app or API
Open weights
download it and run it yourself

One more thing on models. There are basically two camps.

On this side, the frontier, closed models. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok. You can use them, but you can't download them; they run on the company's servers. On this side, the open ones. DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama, Mistral, and all those tools like Whisper and YOLO. You can download them and run them on your own machine, which matters if your data is sensitive.

Okay, let's get practical. Imagine you ask a chatbot: when is my next kulliyyah meeting?

It has no idea. It can't see your calendar, it can't read your emails. It only knows what it learned in training.

And training stops at some point. Everything after that, and everything private to you, it has never seen. Including your newest paper.

So how do we teach it something new? We could train it again, but remember what that costs. Months, millions. So instead, we just give it the information as part of the input. Let me show you.

Demo 1 · try it later
Step by step
  1. Open a chatbotChatGPT, Claude or Gemini
  2. Ask it a general questioncan it answer? yes
  3. Ask it something only you knowe.g. "What did my courtyard paper find?" it can't, or it guesses
  4. Drag and drop your PDF into the chatyour own data
  5. Ask the same question againnow it knows

Here's what I'll do. Just watch for now; every step is on this slide, so you can do it yourself later.

Open any chatbot. ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, whichever you have.

Ask it a general question. Anything. It answers, no problem.

Now ask it something only I know. What did my courtyard paper find? It can't answer. Or worse, it makes something up.

Now drag and drop the paper, the PDF, into the chat. (Have the courtyard PDF ready on the desktop.)

And ask the same question again. Now it knows.

Demo 1 · what we just did
Context engineering
How did we collect our data?
Model
Sorry, I don't know that paper.You observed one campus courtyard, and surveyed students with a questionnaire.from your paper, the method section
the app's instructionsyour paperyour question
question + context = answer
Simplified. The answer comes from the paper's abstract.

So what did we just do? This has a name now: context engineering. Here's the model's context, everything it sees when it answers. The app has already put some instructions in.

First, we asked our question. It goes into the context, the model reads it, and... it doesn't know my paper.

Then I dragged and dropped the PDF. The text of my paper gets put right into the context, before my question.

Now the model reads all of it, and it can answer: we observed one courtyard, and surveyed the students. Straight from the paper. Question plus context equals answer. Notice the model didn't learn anything. Nothing was trained. We just changed what's in front of it. That's context engineering: choosing what goes into the context. Close the chat, and it's gone.

Claude and ChatGPT call it a Project; Gemini calls it a Notebook.

One problem with what we just did: close the chat, and it's gone. Next time, you upload the paper again. So all three big apps now have a place for this: Projects in Claude and ChatGPT, Notebooks in Gemini.

A project is a shared context. You put your files in once: my courtyard paper, my survey data, the conference's call for papers, and you write instructions once. Then every new chat you start inside that project already knows all of it.

Setting one up is simple. Create a project. Add your files. Write some instructions: who it's for, how to answer. And then just chat inside it. Let me show you. (Demo: set up the courtyard project in Claude, then ChatGPT, then a notebook in Gemini.) And every demo after this starts inside this project, so it already knows my paper.

Claude and ChatGPT call it a Project; the new Gemini calls it a Notebook. Different names, same idea. And the same reminder applies: whatever you put in there goes to their servers.

Did you know?
  1. You don't always need a giant modelbig models try to know everything, so they're massive and take months to train. If the job is just finding information in your documents, a smaller model can do it.
  2. Sovereign AIwhose servers, whose rules? Malaysia is building its own: ILMU, and a sovereign AI cloud.

Before you go home and drag and drop everything, a few things you might not know.

A few side notes. First: why are the big models so big? Because they try to know everything, and all of it has to be stored inside those billions of parameters. That's why they're massive, and why they take months to train. But if your job is just finding information, in your papers, your policies, your notes, the model doesn't need to memorise it. It just needs to read what we give it. So a smaller, cheaper model, even one on your own machine, can do the job. And if there are too many documents to fit, we search first and give it only the relevant pieces.

And control. Remember: these run on someone else's servers, under someone else's rules. That's why countries talk about sovereign AI. Malaysia has started with ILMU, a Malaysian language model, and a sovereign AI cloud. And the open models we saw make this possible.

But here's the thing: not all models can output everything.

Claude, for example, is very good at text, but it can't actually draw you an image.

GPT, on the other hand, can give you images. Ask Astra for a picture and you get one.

And Gemini? Gemini gives you everything. Text, pictures, video, music. But notice these are orange. Hold that thought.

Then there are models that only make images,

only make video,

only make audio.

And actually, when Astra gives you a picture, it hands the drawing to a separate image model, GPT Image. One request, more than one model working together. Remember the word cloud? ChatGPT and Gemini are apps; behind each, there are several models. Let me show you how Gemini makes a video.

4 · Output · multimodal
you type

Make a short video of my cat chasing a butterfly.

Geminithe chat model
works out what you want, and calls the right model
Nano Bananapicture model
Omni Flashvideo model
Lyriamusic model
Model names as used in the Gemini app, from Google's Gemini pages (checked 12 Oct 2026). How the app passes work between models is simplified here.

So how does Gemini actually make a video? Say you type: make a short video of my cat chasing a butterfly.

The Gemini you chat with is a language model. Text in, text out, like we saw. So it works out what you want, and calls the right model for the job.

For video, that's a separate video model. Right now it's called Gemini Omni Flash; it just replaced Veo. That's the one that actually makes the video.

Same for pictures: that's Nano Banana. Music: Lyria. So the Gemini app isn't one model doing everything. It's a team of models, and the chat model is the one in the middle, passing the work along. And here's the twist for today: Claude can't draw a picture or make a video by itself. But it can write the code that does. And that's exactly what we're doing in this workshop.

4 · Output · tokens
1token
readingwriting
ModelReading, per 1M tokensWriting, per 1M tokensRead one 10-page paper, write a 1-page summary

Reading a whole paper costs under 1 sen to about 60 sen. Writing costs about 5× more than reading.

Token counts measured with OpenAI's o200k tokenizer on 105 IIUM papers: about 890 per page, 11,600 per paper. API prices checked 4 Oct 2026, at RM 4.08 per US$.

One more thing you'll hear all the time: tokens. Chatbots count, limit and charge everything in tokens. So how much is a token? One token is about one word, or a piece of a word.

Ten tokens is a short sentence.

A hundred, a paragraph.

A thousand tokens is about one page of a journal article.

Ten thousand is about a 10-page paper, one of yours.

A hundred thousand, a whole novel.

And a million tokens? That's about 86 of your papers. Or the first five Harry Potter books. And Malay text uses about twice as many tokens as English for the same meaning, so keep that in mind.

And this is how they charge you. It's priced per million tokens, and reading is cheaper than writing. Usually writing costs about five times more. So for a top model like Claude Opus, reading one of your 10-page papers and writing you a one-page summary costs about 25 sen. The very best models, about 60 sen. The cheap ones, less than one sen. So it's not the cost per question that adds up. It's when you run thousands of them, or when agents run for hours, which we'll get to next.

Demo 2 · images
The mega-prompt
the prompt · 357 words

Transform this SketchUp interior screenshot into a photorealistic interior architectural photograph. The final result must look like a real, built interior space captured with a professional camera.

Maintain the original camera position, angle, framing, and perspective — no extreme camera changes are allowed. Camera must remain consistent with the original view, only minimal natural lens correction is acceptable (no repositioning, no wide distortion).

Strictly preserve the original interior design without any modification:

Do not change layout, furniture placement, proportions, or spatial composition
Do not alter materials, colors, textures, or finishes
All elements (dining table, chairs, wall panels, TV, kitchen set, plants, wall decor, etc.) must remain exactly as shown

The environment and interior elements must be faithfully recreated:

Maintain all furniture positions exactly (dining table, chairs alignment, sofa, TV placement)
Keep wall decorations (including wall clock and map art) exactly the same
Preserve window and door design, including frame details and proportions
Indoor plants must remain in the same position and type (only enhanced to realistic quality, not replaced)

Apply realistic interior lighting:

Natural daylight coming from the windows (soft, diffused tropical light)
Balanced exposure between interior and exterior view
Soft shadows and realistic light bounce (global illumination)

Enhance all materials into true photorealistic quality:

Natural wood grain on flooring, table, and panels
Realistic fabric texture on chairs and sofa
Accurate reflections on glass surfaces and TV screen
Subtle imperfections (fingerprints, slight roughness, micro-texture) for realism
Clean but not overly perfect surfaces

Rendering quality must include:

Global illumination
Ambient occlusion
Physically accurate lighting (PBR workflow)
Realistic reflections and refractions
Depth of field (very subtle, like DSLR)

Atmosphere:

Warm, natural Indonesian residential interior feeling

Neutral, realistic color grading (no dramatic filters)

Keep everything exactly as is:

No adding new objects
No removing elements
No redesign
No style change

Final output:

Photorealistic interior architectural photography
DSLR quality
Ultra-realistic

IMPORTANT NEGATIVE PROMPT:
no camera shift, no extreme angle change, no redesign, no new furniture, no removed objects, no material change, no color change, no style alteration, no overexposed lighting, no unrealistic shadows, no distortion, no wide-angle exaggeration

A real prompt from an architect, to turn a 3D model into a photo-like render.

do you need to write this?

So how do architects do this today? My cousin is an architect. She designs in SketchUp, takes a screenshot like this, and asks an image generator to make it look like a real photo of the finished room.

And this is her prompt. Three hundred and fifty-seven words. Keep the camera, keep the layout, keep the materials, the lighting, global illumination, ambient occlusion, a negative prompt at the end. And it works. This is what people think prompt engineering is: a long, special prompt full of the right words.

But do you need to write this yourself? Not anymore.

Demo 2 · the new way
Prompt engineering: just talk
sketchup.pngI'd like to turn this SketchUp model of a campus courtyard into a realistic photo for my conference poster. Help me build the prompt. Let's talk it through first: what do you need to know to write a complete prompt?
Should the camera, layout, trees and seating stay exactly the same? What time of day, and what light? Should there be people in it?
Keep the design exactly as it is. Late afternoon, soft tropical light. A few students sitting and talking in the shade.
Here's your prompt: "Transform this SketchUp model of a campus courtyard into a photorealistic architectural photograph. Keep the camera angle, layout, trees and seating exactly…"the same kind of prompt, written for you. Then it makes the image.
  • Same result, by talking. You bring the taste; it brings the words.
  • Then fix it in words: "warmer light", "keep the benches".
  • Check it: image tools still change small details.

Here's the new way, for my poster. I've got a SketchUp model of a courtyard. (Grab a courtyard SketchUp screenshot from Google.) I just say what I want, in plain words: I'd like to turn this into a realistic photo for my conference poster, help me build the prompt. And then the important part: let's talk it through first. What do you need to know to write a complete prompt?

And it asks. Should the camera and the layout stay the same? What time of day? Any people? These are exactly the things in her long prompt.

I answer like I'm talking to a colleague. Keep the design. Late afternoon light. And a few students sitting and talking in the shade, because that's what my paper is about.

And it writes the long prompt for me. Camera, layout, materials, lighting, all of it. Then it makes the image.

So you get to the same place, just by talking. You bring the taste, it brings the words. If something's off, say so: warmer light, keep the benches. And check it: image generators still like to change small details, like moving a bench or adding a tree that isn't in the design. That's prompt engineering now: a conversation, not a magic paragraph.

Demo 2 · prompt engineering
What a good prompt covers
  1. What it's for, and who sees it"a hero image for my conference poster"
  2. What it shows"this courtyard, from this exact angle"
  3. What must stay exact"the layout, the trees, the seating"
  4. The look"late-afternoon tropical light, like a real photo"
  5. The format"portrait, high resolution, for an A1 poster" (for a video: how long)
  6. What to avoid"no new buildings, no distortion"

You don't need to remember this list. Ask the AI to interview you, and it asks for all of it.

Works for any task, not just pictures: a grant summary, an exam question, a lesson plan.

So what's actually in a good prompt? Look at what it asked me, and what was in her long prompt. It comes down to six things. What it's for, and who sees it. What it shows. What must stay exactly the same. The look. The format: the size, or for a video, how long. And what to avoid.

But you don't need to remember this list. Ask the AI to interview you, and it will ask you for all six. That's prompt engineering now.

And this works for anything, not just pictures. A grant summary, an exam question, a lesson plan. Same trick.

Here's what I'll do. Again, every step is on the slide.

Ask your chatbot for a diagram. Your research method as a flowchart, or a timeline, or a concept map. I'm still in my courtyard project, so it already knows my method.

But here's the trick: ask for it in draw.io format. Something like this prompt.

Open what it gives you in draw.io, at diagrams.net. It's free, it runs in the browser.

And now it's not a picture, it's a real diagram. You can move the boxes, fix the labels, and export it for your slides or your paper.

And draw.io isn't the only one. Excalidraw gives you a hand-drawn, whiteboard look. Mermaid is a diagram written as a few lines of text; many chatbots can show it to you straight away, and it works in places like GitHub, Notion and Obsidian.

Demo 3
Why this works: a diagram is text
flowchart TD
  A[Observe the courtyard] --> B[Survey the students]
  B --> C[Find the key factors]
Shown: a Mermaid diagram. A draw.io file works the same way, just longer. · mermaid.live

So why does this work, when a chatbot like Claude can't draw a picture?

Because a diagram is just text. This is the simplest kind, Mermaid: one line per box, and an arrow between them. A draw.io file is the same idea, just longer: what each box says, where it sits, and what connects to what.

And text is exactly what these models are good at. So it writes the text, and draw.io or Mermaid turns it into the diagram. Same idea as today's workshop: it can't draw the animation, but it can write the code that draws it.

Recap
Input
Model
Output

What form is it in?

  • image · voice
  • text · numbers

What fits your budget?

  • cost, in ringgit
  • size, 1B to 1T
  • fast or smart?

What do you need back?

  • text · image
  • video · audio
  • code
today: your paper→a frontier chatbot (a few sen)→code → a working animation

So, to recap. Whenever you want to use AI for something, think about three things.

First, the input. What form is your data in? Is it images, voice, text, numbers? Remember, it all has to become numbers in the end.

Second, the model. What's your budget? What size of model do you need? A small one that runs on your laptop, or a big one in the cloud? And there's always a trade-off between speed and performance. The smarter models are slower and cost more; the fast ones are cheaper but less capable.

And third, the output. What do you actually need back? Text? An image? Audio? Or, like today, code?

So for today: your input is your paper. The model is one of these frontier chatbots, and it costs you a few sen. And the output is code, which becomes a working animation of your research.

Part 5
Agents
AI that does things

And now, part five: agents. AI that doesn't just talk, but does things.

5 · Agents
Generative AI generates
WordsImagesVideoSound

and that's it. It talks. It doesn't do.

But what if we let AI do things?

  • search the web
  • run code
  • read and write files
  • fill in a form, send an email

These are called tools.

So far, everything we've seen is generative AI. It generates.

Words, images, video, sound. And that's it. It talks, but it doesn't do anything. You still have to copy the answer, paste it somewhere, click the buttons yourself.

But what if we let it do things? Search the web. Run code. Open and save files. Fill in a form, send an email. Each of these is called a tool. Give a model tools, and it can look at the result and decide what to do next. Here's what that looks like.

5 · Agents
Give a model tools, and it acts
Watch the clipreddit.com/r/Damnthatsinteresting(not bundled: it isn't our video)
  1. He speaks"move left, sweep the area…"
  2. The model picks a toolturn, aim, fire: functions it was given
  3. The machine movesthe result comes back, and it decides what's next

Tools make AI powerful, and that's exactly why who gets which tools matters.

OpenAI Realtime API connected to a motorised rifle mount, Jan 2025 (shared on Reddit, r/Damnthatsinteresting).

(Play the clip.) This went viral last year. Someone connected OpenAI's voice model to a motorised rifle mount. He just talks to it, and it moves. What's happening here: the model has been given a few tools, like turn left, aim, fire. When he speaks, the model decides which tool to call, the machine moves, and it carries on from there.

It's a scary example, on purpose. Give a model tools and it stops just talking; it acts. That's powerful, and it's exactly why we have to think about which tools we give it. For the record, OpenAI cut off his access: weapons are against their usage policy.

5 · Agents
MCP: plugging tools into AI
MCP (Model Context Protocol): one standard way to connect an AI to a tool. In the apps, they're called connectors.
modelcontextprotocol.io

So how do we give a model its tools?

There's now a standard for it, called MCP, the Model Context Protocol. Think of it like a USB port for AI: one standard plug, so any AI app can connect to any tool that supports it.

In Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini you'll see these as connectors. Your Google Drive, Gmail, calendar, GitHub, a database, your own files. Switch one on, and the AI can read from it, or act on it. Remember context engineering? This is the same idea: the AI pulls in exactly the context it needs, by itself.

5 · Agents
The core: the AI writes code to act
You would…The agent writes…In plain words
Look inside a folder→ls papers/list the files in "papers"
Find every PDF from 2025→find . -name "*2025*.pdf"search by file name
Rename 100 files→for f in files: f.rename(...)do it for every file
Make a chart from an Excel sheet→pd.read_excel("data.xlsx").plot()read the sheet, draw the chart
Send an email→gmail.send(to=..., subject=...)use the email tool
Give it the tools, and it can do a lot. Even this slide deck was made as code, in HTML.

Here's the core of agentic AI. How does it actually do things? It writes code. Everything you'd do by hand, it does with a short line of code. You'd open a folder and look inside; it writes "ls", list the files. You'd search for every PDF from 2025; it writes a search command. Rename a hundred files by hand? A three-line loop. A chart from Excel? Code that reads the sheet and draws it. An email? It calls the email tool. So, given the tools, it can do a lot. In fact, this whole slide deck you're looking at was made programmatically. It's a web page, written in HTML, by an AI, from my notes.

So how do you get one of these agents? You don't need to be a programmer. There are coding agents you can just subscribe to.

And Codex, from OpenAI, which comes with ChatGPT Plus and Pro.

The difference from the chat app: these work on your own computer. They can read your files, write code, run it, see the error, and fix it, again and again, until it works. And that's exactly what we're going to use to make a video.

Part 6
Video: pixels or code?
two very different ways to make a video with AI

And now, the core of today: video. And there's one idea I want you to leave with. There are two very different ways AI can make a video: by painting pixels, or by writing code.

6 · Video · pixels or code
Two ways AI can make a video

Pixel video

The AI paints every frame.

your promptvideo modelpictures

It learned from millions of videos. Great at how real things look: people, places, light.

Sora, Veo, Kling, Higgsfield

Code video

The AI writes instructions; the computer draws every frame.

your promptcodepictures

Every picture is calculated. Great when details must be exact: bar("2025", 312) is exactly 312.

Remotion, Claude Motion, HyperFrames

Both are useful, for different jobs.

So, how does AI make a video? Remember, a video is just pictures, shown fast. So who makes all those pictures? There are two very different ways, and this is the most important distinction today.

The first: pixel video. You type a prompt, and a video model paints every frame, pixel by pixel. It has seen millions of videos, so it guesses what each picture should look like. That's Sora, Veo, Kling, Higgsfield. And it's very good at how real things look: people, places, light, camera moves.

The second: code video. The AI doesn't paint anything. It writes instructions, code, and the computer follows them to draw every frame. If the code says this bar is 312, it's exactly 312, in every frame. That's Remotion, which I use today, and Claude Motion, and HyperFrames.

Pixels or code. Both are useful, for different jobs. Keep that in your head for the rest of today. Let's look at each.

6 · Video · pixels
Pixel videos: type a prompt, get a clip

The tools

  • Google Veo, now Gemini Omni
  • OpenAI Sora
  • Kling, Runway, Wan, LTX…
  • Higgsfield: the advanced one, many video models plus camera moves in one place

Great at

  • real-looking footage: people, places, light
  • camera moves and cinematic shots
  • fast: one prompt, one clip

Good for an intro, a promo, b-roll. Our workshop promo opens with pixel video.

First, pixel videos. This is the way most people know: you type a prompt, and you get a video clip. Google's Veo, now Gemini Omni. OpenAI's Sora. Kling, Runway, and open ones like Wan and LTX that we saw earlier. And if you want to go further, Higgsfield: it puts many of these video models in one place, with proper camera moves, like a dolly or a crane shot.

And they're impressive. They learned from millions of videos, so they're great at how real things look: people, places, light, camera moves. And it's fast: one prompt, one clip. We'll compare the two properly in a minute.

So it's great for an intro, a promo, some b-roll. Actually, the promo for this workshop opens with a few seconds of pixel video: the tired lecturer at his desk. The rest of it was code.

So what does that look like? On the left, code. On the right, the video it makes.

The tool that turns this code into an MP4 is called Remotion. The AI writes the code; you, the expert, check the science.

All of this is code.
kos.html · ~570 lines, written by AI
    float fresnel=.035+.965*pow(1.0-facing,5.0);
    vec3 inside=refract(incoming,n,1.0/1.46);
    float distanceInGlass=max(.001,-2.0*radius*dot(n,inside));
    vec3 exitPoint=vWorld+inside*distanceInGlass;
    vec3 exitNormal=normalize(exitPoint-uCentre);
    vec3 outgoing=refract(inside,-exitNormal,1.46);
    float toBackground=clamp((-6.0-exitPoint.z)/min(outgoing.z,-.08),.5,18.0);
    vec4 projected=projectionMatrix*viewMatrix*vec4(exitPoint+outgoing*toBackground,1.0);
    vec2 refractedUV=clamp(projected.xy/projected.w*.5+.5,vec2(.002),vec2(.998));
    vec3 through=texture2D(uBackdrop,refractedUV).rgb;
    vec3 attenuation=exp(-vec3(.18,.073,.042)*distanceInGlass);
    // Internal secondary reflection is a restrained cue to solid thickness.
    vec3 rearReflection=studio(reflect(inside,exitNormal))*.028;
    vec3 colour=through*attenuation*(1.0-fresnel)+rearReflection*attenuation;
    colour+=studio(reflect(incoming,n))*fresnel;

    vec3 start=(uWorldToBead*vec4(vWorld,1.0)).xyz;
    vec3 direction=mat3(uWorldToBead)*inside;
    float stepLength=distanceInGlass/32.0;
    vec3 modeLight=vec3(0.0);
    for(int i=0;i<32;i++){
      float travel=(float(i)+.5)*stepLength;
      vec3 p=start+direction*travel;
      float radial=length(p.xy)-modeRadius;
      float d2=radial*radial+p.z*p.z;
      float core=exp(-d2/.0042);
      float halo=exp(-d2/.0100);
      // Constant angular order and constant field power at all temperatures.
      float angle=atan(p.y,p.x);
      float comet=pow(.5+.5*cos(angle*3.0-uTime*12.0),12.0);
      float fringe=pow(.5+.5*cos(angle*44.0-uTime*20.0),5.0);
      float envelope=(.72+comet*2.7+fringe*.22);
      float field=(core*6.0+halo*.46)*envelope;
      // A local evanescent envelope joins the touching taper to the WGM.
      vec3 coupling=(p-vec3(0.0,-radius+.045,0.0))/vec3(.13,.16,.10);
      field+=exp(-dot(coupling,coupling))*1.8;
      modeLight+=resonanceColour(uHot)*field*stepLength*exp(-travel*.09);
    }
    colour+=modeLight*(1.0-fresnel);
    gl_FragColor=vec4(colour,1.0);
  }`, { side: THREE.FrontSide, transparent: false, depthWrite: true });
const bead = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.SphereGeometry(RADIUS, 96, 64), glass);
bead.renderOrder = 12;
apparatus.add(bead);

const stemProfile = [
  new THREE.Vector2(0,1.69), new THREE.Vector2(.20,1.73),
  new THREE.Vector2(.15,1.84), new THREE.Vector2(.085,2.01),
  new THREE.Vector2(.078,3.15), new THREE.Vector2(.10,3.5)
];
const stem = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.LatheGeometry(stemProfile, 32), shader(`
  varying vec3 vWorld; varying vec3 vNormal;
  void main(){
    vec3 n=normalize(vNormal);vec3 v=normalize(cameraPosition-vWorld);
    float rim=pow(1.0-abs(dot(n,v)),3.0);
    float shine=pow(max(dot(reflect(-v,n),normalize(vec3(-.5,.8,1.0))),0.0),30.0);
    gl_FragColor=vec4(vec3(.08,.18,.22)+vec3(.6,.8,.9)*shine,.12+rim*.5+shine*.3);
  }`));
// The supporting stem is at the POLE, perpendicular to the mode's equator.
stem.rotation.x=Math.PI/2;
stem.renderOrder = 11;
apparatus.add(stem);

const fibreHalfLength = 7.4;
const fibreWaist = .042;
const fibreY = -RADIUS-fibreWaist;
const fibreGeometry = new THREE.BufferGeometry();
const positions = [], normals = [], uvs = [], indices = [];
const fibreSegments = 240, fibreSides = 14;
for (let i=0; i<=fibreSegments; i++) {
  const x = (i/fibreSegments*2-1)*fibreHalfLength;
  const r = fibreWaist+.11*Math.pow(smooth(.8,5.7,Math.abs(x)),1.5);
  for (let j=0;j<=fibreSides;j++) {
    const theta=j/fibreSides*TAU;
    positions.push(x,fibreY+Math.cos(theta)*r,Math.sin(theta)*r);
    normals.push(0,Math.cos(theta),Math.sin(theta));
    uvs.push(i/fibreSegments,j/fibreSides);
    if(i<fibreSegments && j<fibreSides){
      const a=i*(fibreSides+1)+j, b=a+fibreSides+1;
      indices.push(a,a+1,b,b,a+1,b+1);
    }
  }
}
fibreGeometry.setAttribute('position',new THREE.Float32BufferAttribute(positions,3));
fibreGeometry.setAttribute('normal',new THREE.Float32BufferAttribute(normals,3));
fibreGeometry.setAttribute('uv',new THREE.Float32BufferAttribute(uvs,2));
fibreGeometry.setIndex(indices);
const fibre = new THREE.Mesh(fibreGeometry, shader(`
  varying vec3 vNormal; varying vec3 vWorld; varying vec2 vUv;
  uniform float uHot; ${opticalColour}
  void main(){
    vec3 n=normalize(vNormal); vec3 v=normalize(cameraPosition-vWorld);
    float fres=pow(1.0-abs(dot(n,v)),2.5);
    float strip=pow(max(0.0,dot(n,normalize(vec3(0.0,1.0,1.0)))),22.0);
    vec3 col=vec3(.10,.21,.25)+vec3(.5,.76,.83)*strip;
    col+=resonanceColour(uHot)*fres*.36;
    gl_FragColor=vec4(col,.22+.4*fres+.2*strip);
  }`, { side: THREE.DoubleSide }));
fibre.renderOrder = 9;
apparatus.add(fibre);

const fibrePath = new THREE.LineCurve3(new THREE.Vector3(-fibreHalfLength,fibreY,0),new THREE.Vector3(fibreHalfLength,fibreY,0));
const fibreLight = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.TubeGeometry(fibrePath,240,.011,6,false),shader(`
  varying vec2 vUv; uniform float uTime; uniform float uHot; ${opticalColour}
  void main(){
    float x=vUv.x;
    float crest=pow(.5+.5*cos(x*113.0-uTime*23.0),9.0);
    float envelope=.35+.65*pow(.5+.5*cos(x*17.0-uTime*10.0),5.0);
    vec3 col=resonanceColour(uHot);
    // Incoming and outgoing probe show the same tracked resonance colour.
    gl_FragColor=vec4(col*(.65+crest*2.0)*envelope,.9);
  }`,{blending:THREE.AdditiveBlending}));
fibreLight.renderOrder=6;
apparatus.add(fibreLight);

// Magnified transverse electric-field trace at the OUTPUT fibre. Its
// wavelength, not the WGM angular order or optical power, changes with heat.
const waveGeometry=new THREE.PlaneGeometry(4.4,1,420,1);
const waveVertex=`
  uniform float uTime;uniform float uHot;uniform float uWidth;
  varying vec2 vUv;
  void main(){
    vUv=uv;
    float x=position.x+2.45;
    float envelope=smoothstep(.25,.65,x)*(1.0-smoothstep(4.15,4.65,x));
    float wavelength=mix(.32,.90,uHot);
    float phase=(x-.25)*6.28318530718/wavelength-uTime*8.0;
    vec3 p=vec3(x,(${fibreY.toFixed(4)})+position.y*uWidth,
      sin(phase)*.34*envelope);
    gl_Position=projectionMatrix*modelViewMatrix*vec4(p,1.0);
  }`;
const outputWaves=[];
for(const width of [.075,.24]){
  const waveMaterial=new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
    uniforms:{...uniforms,uWidth:{value:width},uAlpha:{value:width<.1?.95:.12}},
    vertexShader:waveVertex,
    fragmentShader:`
      uniform float uHot;uniform float uAlpha;varying vec2 vUv;${opticalColour}
      void main(){
        float crossSection=pow(max(0.0,1.0-abs(vUv.y*2.0-1.0)),1.4);
        float ends=smoothstep(.0,.075,vUv.x)*(1.0-smoothstep(.86,1.0,vUv.x));
        gl_FragColor=vec4(resonanceColour(uHot)*1.8,crossSection*ends*uAlpha);
      }`,transparent:true,depthWrite:false,side:THREE.DoubleSide,
    blending:THREE.AdditiveBlending
  });
  const outputWave=new THREE.Mesh(waveGeometry,waveMaterial);
  outputWave.frustumCulled=false;outputWave.renderOrder=13;
  apparatus.add(outputWave);outputWaves.push(outputWave);
}
A code video: live 3D, from one IIUM paper.Noorbahrin et al. (2025), Results in Optics · Kulliyyah of Science. Illustration, not measured data.

Now let me show you what this can look like when you put in a bit more effort. This is one of the clips I made for this workshop, from a Kulliyyah of Science paper: a tiny glass bead that senses heat with light. And this isn't a video. It's running live, right now, in 3D.

And this is what it's made of. Code. One file, about 570 lines. The AI wrote all of it. I described what I wanted, checked it against the paper, and asked for changes. The glass, the light, the heat, every bit of it is written, not generated.

One IIUM paper, turned into this. It's an illustration, so the colours and the timing are exaggerated to show the idea, but nothing in it is a random guess. That's motion design, with code.

6 · Video · pixels or code
Pixels or code: which one?
Pixel videoCode video
Best forreal-looking footage, people, placesdiagrams, charts, mechanisms, data
Lookphotoreal, cinematicclean, illustrated, 2D or 3D
Numbers and texthit or missexact
Change one detailregenerate, and hopechange one line
Lengthshort clips (~5–15 s), joined upas long as you need
Efforta prompt, a few minutesa conversation with a coding agent, more setup
Costcredits per clip; good quality costs morean AI subscription; the video tools are free for individuals

How it looks → pixels.   What's exact → code.   Many projects use both.

For research and teaching, exactness usually matters most. That's why today's demo uses code.

So now we've seen both. Let's be fair and put them side by side. Pixel video is best for real-looking footage, people, places. Code video is best for diagrams, charts, mechanisms, data. Pixels look photoreal; code looks clean and illustrated, though it can be 3D too. Numbers and text: hit or miss with pixels, exact with code. To change one detail, with pixels you regenerate and hope; with code you change one line. Pixel clips are short, so you join them up; code can be as long as you need. Pixel video is faster to start, just a prompt. Code takes a conversation with a coding agent and a bit more setup. And both cost something: with pixels you pay credits per clip, and the good-quality models cost more; with code you need an AI subscription, though the video tools themselves are free for individuals.

So a simple rule. If it's about how it looks, pixels. Like my poster image. If it's about what's exact, code. Like the video for my talk. And many projects use both, like our promo.

For research and teaching, exactness usually matters most. That's why today's demo uses code.

Like our promo. Here's how I made the promo you saw at the start: pixels and code.

I started in Claude Code. Not with code: with the idea. What do I want to show, which examples, what's the story. Together we drafted an outline, shot by shot.

Then for each shot, one question: pixel or code? The tired lecturer at his desk at 2 a.m. has to look real, so that's pixels: an AI image, then animated into a short clip. The research animations, the captions, the end card with the date and venue: those have to be exact, so that's code.

Then I made the parts. The pixel shots with an image generator and a video model. The code scenes with Claude Code and Remotion.

And then I put it all together and polished it in Claude Code: the timing, the music, the voice, which were also AI-made. And iterate, iterate. Watch it, say what's wrong, fix, watch again.

Demo 4 · tip
Tip: show, don't describe
Here's my paper, and a screenshot of a style I like. Make my video look like this.
  • colours, layout, fonts and mood, all in one picture
  • works with any demo, a journal figure, a YouTube frame

A picture beats a paragraph. Screenshot what you like, and say "like this".

A tip for the prompt, my favourite. Describing a style in words is hard. So don't. Show it.

Find a demo you like, take a screenshot, and attach it with your paper. "Make my video look like this."

One picture carries the colours, the layout, the fonts, the mood. It works with anything: a demo like this, a figure from a journal you admire, a frame from a YouTube explainer. For my talk, I'd attach the poster image from demo two, so the video matches the poster.

A picture beats a paragraph. Screenshot what you like and say "like this". You'll see the same trick again in step 4, with a screenshot of a mistake. It saves a lot of back and forth.

And I say: read the paper, use the prompt we agreed on, and show me a plan of the scenes before you write any code.

Why a plan first? Because this is where I catch mistakes. Are these the design factors the paper actually found? Is that the right number from the table? Fixing a plan takes one sentence. Fixing a finished video takes longer. When the plan looks right, I say: go ahead, build it.

Bonus
Bonus: a textbook question, animated
Question 5

A ball is kicked from flat ground at 20 m/s, at 30° above the horizontal. Ignore air resistance and take g = 9.8 m/s².

  1. How long is the ball in the air?
  2. How high does it go?
  3. How far away does it land?

One last bonus. Here's a typical question from a physics worksheet. A ball kicked at 20 metres per second, 30 degrees. How long in the air, how high, how far. Students usually just get this: a static picture and a formula.

Now the same question, as a simulation. (Press Play.) Each dot is a tenth of a second apart. Watch the arrows: the sideways speed never changes, the upward speed shrinks, hits zero at the top, then points down. Two seconds in the air, about 5 metres high, lands about 35 metres away. Same as the worksheet answer. Now let's play. Try 60 degrees... it lands in exactly the same spot. Why? That's the question to ask your students. Then try 45.

Bonus
Make one for your class
  1. Ask for a simulationone HTML file, with sliders for the things students should change
  2. Open it in a browserno installing, works offline
  3. Check the sciencetry the extremes: zero, very large, negative
  4. Share the fileemail it, put it on your course page, or host it as a link
try this

Turn this textbook question into an interactive simulation, as a single HTML file. Show the ball's path with a dot every tenth of a second, and its velocity as arrows. Add a Play button and sliders for speed and angle, and keep earlier paths so students can compare.

And you can make these for your own class, the same way.

Ask for a simulation as one HTML file, and say which things students should be able to change. Paste in the question itself, or a photo of the worksheet, and ask for it as a simulation. Something like this.

Open it in the browser. Nothing to install, and it works offline.

Then check the science. Push the sliders to the extremes. Zero, very large, negative. That's usually where a simulation breaks, and where you'll catch mistakes.

And share it. It's just a file: email it, put it on your course page, or host it as a link. Your students get something they can play with, not just watch.

One last thing
AI moves fast: keep track of the meta

Code is cheap now

One developer used AI to rebuild free, open-source versions of the Adobe suite:

PhotoCraftPhotoshop
FilmCraftPremiere
VectorCraftIllustrator
LightCraftLightroom

ArtCraft, Oct 2026. Early alpha, still buggy.

Remotion isn't the only one

  • Motion Canvas: code-driven animation, made for explainer videos
  • Revideo: a fork of Motion Canvas, built for automated rendering
  • HyperFrames: from HeyGen; write HTML, render video. Fully open source
  • Manim: the Python library behind 3Blue1Brown's maths videos

Today's best tool may not be next month's. Check what's current before you commit.

ArtCraft by Brandon Thomas (PetaPixel, Oct 2026) · motioncanvas.io · github.com/redotvideo/revideo · www.manim.community

One last thing before I let you go: AI is moving very fast.

Because writing code is so cheap now, people are rebuilding whole products. Just this month, one developer used AI to build free, open-source versions of Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, Lightroom and more. They're early and buggy, but a single person did that, in months.

Same for our tools. I use Remotion, but there are others. Motion Canvas, made for explainer videos. Revideo, built on Motion Canvas for automated rendering. And Manim, the Python library behind the 3Blue1Brown maths videos.

So keep track of the meta. What's best today may not be best next month. Before you commit to a tool, spend five minutes checking what people are using now.
